question:
Patient note:
A 30-year-old woman who works as a warehouse inventory coordinator and coaches a community girls’ basketball team after hours was referred to the combined hematology–pulmonary clinic this morning for a pre-induction assessment of recently diagnosed precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and concurrent review of her long-standing respiratory and metabolic conditions before she begins an intensive chemotherapy protocol next week. She reports that for the past fifteen years she has carried rescue albuterol wherever she goes, originally prescribed during high-school track meets when exercise routinely provoked chest tightness and audible wheeze; over the last five years spirometry has demonstrated a persistently reduced FEV1/FVC ratio with only partial reversibility after bronchodilator, most recently measuring a pre-bronchodilator FEV1 of 2.1 L (68 % predicted), FVC of 3.6 L (87 % predicted), and FEV1/FVC of 0.58, improving to 0.62 fifteen minutes after administration of 400 µg salbutamol, and her outside pulmonologist labeled the pattern consistent with chronic airway limitation related to a combination of childhood asthma and cigarette exposure from a brief two-pack-year history in college. Maintenance therapy has included budesonide–formoterol 160/4.5 µg two inhalations twice daily plus montelukast nightly, with flares requiring short prednisone tapers roughly twice per winter; she has never required hospital admission or intubation, and today she arrives breathing comfortably, speaking in full sentences, and saturating 97 % on room air. Cardiovascular review is otherwise silent: she denies squeezing substernal pain, diaphoresis out of proportion to exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, palpitations, or syncope, and a screening echocardiogram obtained by the oncology team last week displayed normal chamber sizes, a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 63 %, and no valvular abnormality; N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide measured 42 pg/mL, and a high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I level was <6 ng/L, with a contemporaneous 12-lead ECG showing normal sinus rhythm without Q waves or ischemic changes. She similarly recounts no episode of unilateral weakness, slurred speech, facial droop, visual blackout, or gait imbalance. Endocrine history reveals that at age twenty-seven, during an employee wellness fair, fasting plasma glucose measured 145 mg/dL on two separate occasions and hemoglobin A1c was 7.4 %; her most recent hemoglobin A1c two weeks ago was 6.8 %, and since then she has taken metformin 1000 mg twice daily, logs carbohydrate intake on a smartphone application, and brings finger-stick readings that cluster between 100 and 150 mg/dL before breakfast; a spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio last month was 12 mg/g. She denies visual blurring, numbness in the feet, change in vibration sense, renal colic, or non-healing ulcers, and an ophthalmology note from six months ago documented a clear retina without microaneurysms. The leukemia was discovered three weeks ago when she sought care for prolonged bruising on her shins, fatigue after climbing one flight of stairs, and intermittent low-grade fevers; complete blood count at an urgent-care clinic showed white cells 85 × 10⁹/L with 80 % lymphoblasts, hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, and platelets 38 × 10⁹/L. Bone-marrow aspirate confirmed the diagnosis and revealed a t(12;21) translocation; she has received no cytotoxic agents yet, only allopurinol for tumor-lysis prophylaxis and a single dose of dexamethasone for laryngeal edema after mediastinal biopsy. Baseline hepatic panel drawn yesterday demonstrated alanine aminotransferase 58 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 52 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 78 U/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, albumin 4.1 g/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.0. An abdominal ultrasound performed at diagnosis described a mildly enlarged, diffusely echogenic liver without nodularity, patent portal and hepatic veins, no splenomegaly, and absence of ascites; she has never manifested jaundice, encephalopathy, gastro-intestinal bleeding, pruritus, or abdominal distention. Kidney function today is intact—sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 12 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate 112 mL/min/1.73 m², and urinalysis is bland. She denies heartburn, coffee-ground emesis, melena, or prior ulcer therapy, uses ibuprofen only during menses, and takes no proton-pump inhibitor. An HIV antigen/antibody screen obtained at the time of leukemia work-up was non-reactive. Current medication list therefore includes metformin, budesonide–formoterol, montelukast, albuterol as needed (one inhaler lasts about two months), allopurinol 300 mg daily since last week, and a combined ethinyl-estradiol/levonorgestrel oral contraceptive to regulate irregular cycles exacerbated by systemic corticosteroid bursts; she reports no drug allergies. Socially, she lives in a small apartment with her twin sister, jogs two miles three times weekly when fatigue allows, quit smoking eight years ago, consumes two glasses of wine per month, and has never used recreational drugs. Family pedigree reveals a father with type 2 diabetes diagnosed in his forties, a mother with childhood-onset asthma, and no relatives with leukemia, cirrhosis, myocardial infarction before age sixty, or stroke. Vital signs on arrival: temperature 37.1 °C, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg seated, heart rate 92 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, body-mass index 26 kg/m² (height 165 cm, weight 70.8 kg). Examination finds a well-oriented woman with scattered petechiae over the forearms, supple neck without lymphadenopathy, brisk carotid upstrokes, jugular venous pulsation estimated at 3 cm above the sternal angle, normal first and second heart sounds without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, lungs clear at bases with faint expiratory wheezes in upper fields, abdomen soft with a smooth liver edge palpable 1 cm below the costal margin and no splenic tip, and extremities without edema. Neurologic testing shows intact cranial nerves II–XII, full strength, symmetric reflexes, preserved sensation, and steady tandem gait. She seeks clarification regarding timing of induction chemotherapy relative to her glucose control, guidance on preventive inhaler adjustments during expected neutropenic isolation, and counselling on hepatoprotective measures while receiving potentially hepatotoxic agents.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums age points and weighted comorbidities present at baseline.
- Age 30: Under 50, so 0 points.
- Chronic pulmonary disease: Persistent airflow obstruction requiring maintenance inhalers qualifies, even though she is comfortable today: 1 point.
- Uncomplicated diabetes: She takes metformin, with no documented nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy, or other diabetic end-organ damage: 1 point.
- Mild liver disease: Diffuse hepatic echogenicity with mild aminotransferase elevation supports fatty liver disease. Synthetic function is preserved, with no evidence of portal hypertension: 1 point.
- Leukemia: Marrow-confirmed acute lymphoblastic leukemia is present before induction: 2 points.
No other qualifying comorbidity is documented. Total = 0 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 5.
Final answer: 5
